lines.text: At five in the morning, a mountain in Missouri began to pour itself into a valley.
A billion gallons of water. In twelve minutes.
And at the bottom, a family was asleep.
This is the Tom Sauk reservoir.
A man-made lake on top of Proffit Mountain, built to store electricity.
It was watched, every night, by a few small water gauges.
And those gauges were wrong.
The idea was simple.
At night, when power was cheap, pumps pushed water up the mountain.
By day, it rushed back down through turbines to make electricity.
A giant battery, made of water and rock.
The lake was ringed by a wall of piled rock, topped with concrete.
The plant relied on gauges hung inside pipes on the wall.
When the water reached the line, the pumps switched off.
But there was a problem.
The pipes had worked loose from their brackets.
The gauges inside had slipped.
So they read the water lower than it really was.
By about two feet.
There was a backup. Two emergency probes, ready to shut everything down.
But they had been set too high.
Above the lowest point of the wall.
Nobody noticed. Not yet.
December the fourteenth, two thousand and five.
The pumps ran through the night, as they always did.
The gauges said there was room to spare.
There wasn't.
Just after five, water began spilling over the low spots of the wall.
Minutes later, a section nearly seven hundred feet wide simply gave way.
The flood tore down the mountain, scraping it to bare stone.
It poured into Johnson's Shut-Ins State Park.
Straight through the home of the superintendent, Jerry Toops.
Jerry, his wife Lisa, and their three children were swept away inside it.
All five survived.
The children were pulled from the wreckage cold, but alive.
The rock had not failed first. The readings had.
The owner paid around a hundred and eighty million dollars, and rebuilt it in concrete.
The wall did exactly what it was told.
It was just told the wrong number.
